content: Individuals may have acquired HIV in the past due to behaviors such as using contaminated needles or engaging in unprotected sex, but they may no longer engage in these behaviors. Therefore, identifying someone as part of a key population at a single point in time may not be relevant or useful for future patient management or program monitoring. HIV prevention services can be provided without collecting personally identifiable information by using anonymous unique identifier (UID) codes for longitudinal monitoring. However, in most settings, individuals receiving HIV treatment must be identified. Due to the sensitivity of information that could reveal engagement in stigmatized or criminalized behaviors or key population status, only clinically relevant information should be included in clinical records where individuals are personally identified. Relevant clinical information, such as alcohol or drug dependence, concomitant medications (including opioid agonist maintenance therapy [OAMT] and hormone therapy), and sexual risk behavior, should be securely recorded as it is pertinent to clinical care. In settings where stigma is a concern, collecting data on stigmatized behaviors may have limited value, as individuals are unlikely to report such behaviors. Important clinical information related to key populations that could be recorded on the HIV patient card includes whether the patient is receiving OAMT or hormone therapy at the antiretroviral therapy (ART) clinic or elsewhere, or whether alcohol/substance use is a reason for non-adherence to ART. Counseling, support, or education on these and other relevant interventions (e.g., partner testing, couples counseling, preor post-exposure prophylaxis for partners of those on ART) may be addressed and recorded on the back of the HIV patient card by counselors, clinicians, or other health workers. ART registers, which are accessible to various facility staff, may not ensure confidentiality. Therefore, they are not suitable for collecting data related to key population status. Ensuring sufficient ART coverage among key populations living with HIV is critical for a successful HIV response. Routine program data reported to subnational and national data management units should not include key population categories or risk behaviors if this information can be linked to an individual. De-identified case surveillance data, disaggregated by probable transmission route collected at diagnosis, can serve as a proxy for key population groups to measure the impact of HIV programs and estimate the number and proportion of key population members covered at different points in the HIV care cascade. In some settings, key population-specific programs that refer HIV-positive individuals to health services for treatment and care may maintain records of referred individuals. These programs may review ART registers to determine whether referrals were completed and whether individuals received ART, provided safeguards are in place to protect client identity and confidentiality. For example, in Malawi, the EpiC program supports HIV services for key populations. When a client is referred from an EpiC program to a public health facility for HIV treatment, a referral ticket is completed in triplicate. Two tickets are given to the client, and one is retained by the program. At the facility, the healthcare provider signs both tickets, indicates the service received (e.g., ART prescribed), and records the UID used to identify the client in the facility register. One ticket is deposited in a referral ticket box at the facility, and the other is returned to the client for their next visit to the EpiC program. Twice a month, EpiC clinicians or monitoring and evaluation officers collect referral tickets from public health facilities to ascertain completed referrals. They review ART registers to identify key population clients and track retention in care, ART adherence, and viral load suppression. This individual-level data is added to the client’s EpiC program record, enabling the program to monitor HIV treatment outcomes and generate HIV testing, treatment, and care cascades. At no point is the client’s key population status disclosed or recorded in public health facility ART registers or the HIV patient card. The system includes redundancies to improve the likelihood of tracking clients across the EpiC program and public health facilities. Transgender and gender-diverse individuals are those whose gender identity and expression do not align with the norms traditionally associated with their sex assigned at birth. Gender identity categories may include male, female, and other (e.g., trans and gender-diverse individuals who choose an identity other than male or female). In settings where being trans or gender-diverse is highly stigmatized or penalized, it is acceptable to include only two categories (male or female) for gender on facility records to enhance client safety. In other settings, it may be appropriate to include two questions when recording gender on clinical records: (1) Gender (male, female, other) and (2) Sex assigned at birth (male, female, other). These questions allow for better patient management and data disaggregation by gendered groups. The minimum dataset for HIV care includes core demographic, clinical, and laboratory data with standardized definitions and coding categories. This dataset comprehensively assesses all individuals living with HIV who are tested and receiving care. Its primary purpose is to standardize patient information with a simplified and harmonized set of essential data elements relevant to patient management and program monitoring. Standardization enables program staff to compare data across populations, time, geographical areas, and settings, and provides clinical teams with data to monitor care quality longitudinally and along the HIV service cascade. The 2022 WHO minimum dataset for HIV testing and treatment includes updates reflecting the latest WHO recommendations. These updates include new ARV regimens, monitoring of rapid ART initiation, tracking disengagement from care, and monitoring advanced HIV disease. Laboratory data updates include viral load and CD4 monitoring recommendations, while clinical data updates include comorbidities, immunizations, and developmental disorders in children. The dataset also includes elements to monitor adverse pregnancy outcomes associated with ARV exposure and tailored adherence counseling for individuals with advanced HIV disease or unsuppressed viral loads. Key terms and definitions for HIV patient monitoring include newly enrolled in HIV care, which refers to individuals with a confirmed HIV diagnosis who present to a facility or community ART site for the first time. WHO recommends rapid ART initiation within seven days of diagnosis. Retention in care refers to individuals enrolled in HIV care who routinely attend services as appropriate to their needs, excluding those who have died or are lost to follow-up. Understanding retention is critical for assessing progress toward achieving the second 95 target in the HIV care cascade.
